articles.author: calvin-rook
articles.title: The Rook Board: start with the job each club needs filled
articles.dek: Fortree compares protection with coverage, Eterna needs offensive help, and all 32 clubs get a first scouting agenda before the offseason changes it.

body.text: Fortree should spend its first serious draft meeting comparing protection with coverage. The Skyhawks have taken forty-six sacks and allowed 341 points through thirteen games. I ranked Marshadow first on last week’s board, and I still want Fortree to study him. I also want Agate State’s Lapras in the conversation before anyone decides that a spectacular defensive-back workout automatically ends the discussion.

This week’s board asks which jobs each club should investigate. The priorities are my judgments from visible production, recorded games and confirmed availability. Team totals identify questions; they do not assign every sack to an offensive lineman or every conceded point to a cornerback. A useful scouting meeting compares the possible causes, the available prospects and the role the newcomer would actually receive.

Marshadow’s 85–99 scouting band, 4.55 forty and 6.10 cone justify serious attention at cornerback. The Gateon State prospect leads my current board because the combination is unusually attractive. Fortree has just followed a seventy-nine-point defeat with a much more competitive 29–23 loss. Coverage remains worth improving even after a better afternoon, and the first game does not establish exactly which defender a rookie should replace.

Lapras offers a different answer. Agate State’s offensive-line prospect has a 77–99 band, a 4.95 forty and seventeen bench repetitions. Those numbers earn an examination of the protection job. They do not prove that Lapras can eliminate sacks, because quarterback decisions, receiver availability and the opponent’s rush all affect the result. Forty-six sacks are still enough reason for Fortree to make the examination a priority.

I would put Marshadow and Lapras through the work their proposed jobs demand, then compare the improvement available at each position. That is a better draft argument than announcing that the team with the worse defense must always choose a defender. The Skyhawks need both sides to become more dependable, and the best available improvement may depend on which player is actually within reach when their selection arrives.
Contenders can plan beyond this week

Mossdeep has scored 597 points and allowed 117. A team with that production can be selective about the developmental role it creates. The continuing absences of cornerback Marshall Flock and safety Luvrelle Revis make secondary depth a reasonable investigation, while the offense’s sustained success makes future protection worth preserving. Neither concern implies that the Eclipse should replace a successful starter simply to give a prospect an impressive label.

Saffron and Mt. Silver have similar freedom to examine succession with patience. Saffron has made fifty sacks and allowed fourteen; the Reds have allowed only 105 points. Those results should make a club more careful about displacing useful players. A rookie needs a real opportunity to become useful. Carrying an attractive prospect without a credible job is a considerably less exciting plan once the first practice arrives.

Sunyshore’s new Serp Gardener absence puts coverage depth in the current conversation. The draft is a later decision, and a two-week injury counter cannot decide the entire next season. Karson Jones should ask whether a cornerback prospect adds a durable option after the present injury clears. The same distinction applies to Olivine’s receiving absences and Canalave’s injured backs.
Give the offense a useful next answer

Eterna has allowed 137 points and scored 157. Its thirty-four sacks taken, including seven at Pastoria, make protection one of the clearest investigations on this sheet. I would compare Lapras, Eiscue and the other linemen directly, then assess whether a receiving outlet changes the quarterback’s available answers. A new blocker and a reliable short target can address related problems through different jobs.

Canalave has produced 1,190 passing yards and 128 points. That deserves a broader passing-game review than simply circling a quarterback on the board. The receiving options, protection and intended distribution of work belong in the same conversation. With Gabite and Nidoking unavailable now, the club also has a visible reminder to examine how its rushing plan survives absences. Those are connected personnel questions, and the draft should be judged by the improvement it can plausibly supply.

Mauville’s 2,743 passing yards have produced only 162 team points. I want a careful look at rushing help and protection before another offseason is spent admiring yardage that does not become enough scoring. University of Mauville’s Shuckle will receive local attention, naturally. The 66–94 band warrants evaluation; familiarity with the university does not settle how the prospect would block for this particular offense.

The table names primary comparisons rather than confirmed vacancies. It uses current production and availability, without assuming future trades, free-agent signings or draft order. Each club should revisit the priorities after the season and after it knows which players it will retain. The prospect cards below identify useful comparisons in the current visible class. No rookie named here can repair a Week 15 absence.

body.title: First scouting questions for all 32 clubs
body.caption: Through Week 14 · editorial priorities from observed production and availability

cells: Test whether a stronger interior run defender changes the manageable downs available to opponents before assigning every failure to the secondary.
Look for a target who can keep short possessions moving, then compare protection help. Heatmor’s new absence highlights depth, but next season’s role must survive his recovery.
Investigate receivers who can create useful gains without requiring a complete change in the offense; compare a back who supports the same possession goal.
Protect the productive passing game while testing whether a new runner can broaden the offense. A prospect’s listed position alone cannot settle the blocking problem.
Compare an edge prospect and a runner on the same value sheet. The late passing success against Cinnabar provides a reason to support the offense rather than replacing its identity.
414 points scored, 14 sacks taken and 50 sacks made.
Use the freedom created by a strong roster to examine future protection and target depth. Demand a credible playing role before selecting a development project.
Start with protection and compare the running-game alternatives. The passing yardage needs to become more reliable scoring possessions.
Evaluate both protection and coverage before deciding which side offers the larger improvement. Points allowed identifies a broad problem, not a particular defender’s responsibility.
1,742 rushing yards allowed and 28 sacks taken.
Put the front-seven candidates through run assignments first. The offense also needs fewer difficult passing downs; both lines deserve a direct comparison.
21 sacks made, 19 sacks taken and only 105 points allowed.
A strong defense can still compare new pressure options. Keep the existing success in view and require any rookie to justify displacing a useful player.
169 points scored and 1,223 rushing yards allowed.
Receiving absences make depth visible now, while the season run-defense record makes the interior worth investigating for next year. Avoid treating a temporary absence as the entire draft plan.
Evaluate who can add useful completions to a productive rushing base. Haunter’s absence sharpens the current concern, but readiness and future workload must be assessed separately.
Compare protection help with a runner who can keep the offense out of repeated passing situations. The goal is more sustained possessions, not simply another name in the backfield.
17 sacks made, 2,067 passing yards and 201 points scored.
Travis Scarboro should examine a pressure contributor and a target who helps whichever quarterback earns the job. The latest win offers breathing room for a careful comparison.
Investigate a target who adds to the rushing foundation. Golduck’s injury makes tight-end depth worth checking without assuming the long-term answer must occupy that same position.
3,541 passing yards, 30 sacks taken and 1,318 rushing yards allowed.
Support the productive passing attack while testing the run-defense alternatives. A successful record does not make either comparison unnecessary.
1,924 rushing yards, 1,920 passing yards and 15 sacks made.
Pressure help is my first comparison. Then examine a receiving option that complements the strong running production rather than duplicating a job already filled.
30 sacks taken, including seven in the latest loss.
Begin with the protection review and compare a target who offers useful outlets. Mossdeep supplied a severe test; the season sack total prevents dismissing it as the entire story.
The rushing foundation has produced 1,514 yards. Compare pressure help against a receiver who makes that foundation easier to sustain when opponents force a throw.
698 rushing yards, 2,743 passing yards and 162 points scored.
Calvin wants the passing production converted into more points. Investigate a runner and protection help, then test which addition changes actual possession outcomes.
Keep two investigations open. The defense needs more successful passing downs, and the offense needs fewer sacks; a single poor result cannot identify the best draft position by itself.
Fortree should compare the best available protection prospect directly with the best coverage prospect. Both problems are large enough to deserve premium attention.
597 points scored and 117 allowed; Flock and Revis remain unavailable.
The current absences show why credible coverage depth matters. Compare that job with future protection while preserving the productive offense’s existing roles.
14 sacks made, 592 rushing yards and 283 points allowed.
Start with a defender who can affect passing downs, while checking whether a runner can produce a more reliable offensive alternative. Kingdra’s new absence adds a separate coverage-depth question.
1,757 passing yards, 165 points scored and 19 sacks made.
Compare a useful receiving role with pressure help. A rookie must earn a job that changes these outputs rather than merely fitting a position label.
34 sacks taken, 157 points scored and only 137 allowed.
The defense has supplied enough support to make offense the first investigation. Protection and accessible completions should be evaluated together.
Compare quarterback and receiver options before assigning the shortage to one player. Gabite and Nidoking’s absences also make the depth of the rushing plan visible.
Study both sides of the passing-down exchange. The best selection should have a realistic job, with the development time stated plainly.
Compare coverage prospects against a receiving addition that helps sustain drives. The 27-point win this week is useful evidence, not a complete season repair.
Begin with candidates who can turn ordinary possessions into scoring opportunities. Compare actual roles before committing to a quarterback change from team totals alone.
144 points scored, 27 sacks taken and 31 sacks made.
The latest seven-sack defensive performance increases the value of offensive support. Evaluate protection and another reliable target before adding to an already productive pressure group.
322 points scored, 589 rushing yards allowed and a new Gardener absence.
Coverage depth is worth examining while the broader team performs well. Compare it with future protection and resist drafting solely around a short injury counter.

prospects.name: Marshadow
prospects.analysis: Marshadow remains my first coverage evaluation. The 85–99 band accompanies a 4.55 forty and a 6.10 cone, a combination worth testing against a demanding cornerback assignment. Fortree has the strongest immediate case for investigating him, while Mossdeep and Sunyshore can examine whether the role and eventual availability justify the investment.
prospects.concern: Workout movement does not establish coverage judgment or a guaranteed starting role.
prospects.projection: Cornerback comparison for Fortree; depth-and-succession evaluation for Mossdeep and Sunyshore.

prospects.name: Lapras
prospects.analysis: Lapras gives Fortree and Eterna a high-band protection candidate to compare with the defensive alternatives. The 77–99 range is attractive, while a 4.95 forty and seventeen bench repetitions provide useful movement and strength questions for the blocking evaluation.
prospects.concern: Protection performance requires direct football evaluation; sack totals have several causes.
prospects.projection: Offensive-line evaluation for Fortree, Eterna, Petalburg and Vermilion.

prospects.name: Eiscue
prospects.analysis: Eiscue’s 71–99 band, 4.95 forty and nineteen bench repetitions make the Paniola State lineman a serious comparison with Lapras. I would put both through the same intended job before deciding which workout difference matters.
prospects.concern: The range is broad and does not establish immediate readiness.
prospects.projection: Alternative offensive-line evaluation for clubs prioritizing protection.

prospects.name: Iron Bundle
prospects.analysis: Iron Bundle’s 4.53 forty, forty-seven-inch vertical and 5.96 cone remain among my favorite workout combinations. Rustboro and Cerulean should compare the outside linebacker with other ways of improving passing downs, using the 69–97 band as an invitation to examine rather than a completed answer.
prospects.concern: The workout does not prove pass-rush technique, coverage skill or every-down suitability.
prospects.projection: Pressure-role investigation for Rustboro, Cerulean, Lavender and Sootopolis.

prospects.name: Granbull
prospects.analysis: Granbull offers a 65–93 band at defensive tackle with a 5.01 forty and fifteen bench repetitions. Azalea’s 1,742 rushing yards allowed make interior run assignments a sensible starting point for its evaluation.
prospects.concern: Team rushing yards allowed cannot identify one defender’s responsibility or prove the prospect solves it.
prospects.projection: Interior comparison for Azalea, Blackthorn and Viridian.

prospects.name: Miltank
prospects.analysis: Miltank’s 65–93 band comes with twenty-two bench repetitions and a 4.72 forty. I want Mauville and Cerulean to compare the halfback with protection improvements, because either route might better support their passing production.
prospects.concern: The combine does not establish ball security, receiving reliability or actual rushing efficiency.
prospects.projection: Halfback comparison for Mauville, Cerulean and clubs reviewing rushing depth.

prospects.name: Dhelmise
prospects.analysis: Dhelmise’s 80–99 band and twenty-eight bench repetitions demand a serious tight-end evaluation. The 5.06 forty suggests a different conversation from a pure speed target. Pastoria, Cianwood and Veilstone should investigate what receiving-and-blocking workload would make the selection useful.
prospects.concern: A strong band and bench result do not supply route or blocking technique.
prospects.projection: Tight-end and receiving-support comparison after the intended role is defined.

prospects.name: Shuckle
prospects.analysis: Shuckle’s 66–94 band keeps the University of Mauville prospect in the line conversation. The 5.19 forty and sixteen bench repetitions offer less athletic glamour than some alternatives, which makes the actual blocking evaluation especially important.
prospects.concern: Local familiarity and a favorable range do not establish the best fit.
prospects.projection: Mauville should compare its local lineman directly with Lapras and Eiscue rather than treating the choice as sentimental.
